pending_items.title: Protests in Iraqi Kurdistan at plans for government in Baghdad to take over oil, border crossings
pending_items.content:
Protesters took to the streets of Irbil, also often written Erbil, in Iraqi Kurdistan early on Thursday in large numbers, waving massive flags of the semiautonomous region in northern Iraq .

They were responding to federal government plans announced earlier in the week for Baghdad to take control of oil operations and border crossings previously run by Kurdish authorities.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi had said the measures were part of a bid to stop oil smuggling when announcing the changes.

The plans marked an escalation in the long-running power struggle between the central government and Kurdish authorities that have largely governed themselves since 1991, albeit with varying levels of recognition and authority.

Rival Kurdish parties joined forces for the large protests in the regional capital.

Protests were also reported to have spread to several other towns and cities beyond the capital.

Iraq's 2005 constitution, written following the US-led invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein, formally recognized the Kurdish region and its government. But authorities in Erbil and Baghdad have remained in a tug of war over the control of land, oil and money ever since.

Tuesday's decision, which received backing from Iraq's Federal Supreme Court a day later, brings border crossing in the Kurdish region under federal government management. It places approval for oil exports from the region under the authority of the federal oil ministry and transfers the management of oil fields in four contested provinces — Kirkuk, Diyala, Salahuddin and Nineveh.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Kurdish regional government's Cabinet said on Wednesday that the decision from Baghdad "violates both the Constitution and the constitutional rights of the Kurdistan region," saying it represented "an attempt to return Iraq to a centralized regime."

Prime Minister al-Zaidi, who took office earlier this year with the backing of US President Donald Trump, also dismissed Kirkuk's operations commander and police chief and the head of the Border Ports Commission. He said the measures reflected Iraq's "independent national will."

Regional Prime Minister Masrour Barzani said his government was "surprised" by al-Zaidi's decisions and called them "completely unacceptable."

Iraq's Supreme Court ruled on Wednesday that the authority of the Kurdish Regional Government (KRG) only covered the land it administered on March 19, 2003, the day before the US-led invasion that unseated Saddam Hussein.

Kurdish peshmerga forces moved into many disputed areas after 2003, including the oil fields covered by this week's orders.

The 2005 constitution tried to solve the fate of some of the disputed territories in the lands between the borders to Syria and Iran that are home to a host of ethnicities and communities but with Kurds generally the majority group.

Article 140 called for reversing Saddam-era policies of expelling Kurds and moving Arabs in, and called for a census and a referendum on whether the disputed regions should join the Kurdistan region. Neither was held.

Kurdish forces then gained more of the disputed territory after Iraqi forces were forced out by the so-called "Islamic State," with Kurdish pershmerga for subsequently reclaiming some of the land with some international assistance .

The oil-rich region is highly important to both administrations, in a country that relies on oil revenues for the vast majority of its public sector budget.

Internal political tensions within Iraqi Kurdistan have further complicated the issue in recent months, with the Federal Supreme Court hearing an ongoing challenge against the current government's legitimacy after a party withdrew from the coalition cabinet. But rival Kurdish political factions seem to have found common ground on this issue at least.

pending_items.title: Two Italians killed by ‘drone strike debris’ in Kuwait
pending_items.content:
Two Italians have died from their injuries in Kuwait, after being hit by falling debris as authorities said they tried to intercept incoming Iranian drones.

Kuwait’s Ministry of Defence said two other workers, a Kuwaiti and a Pakistani national, were also wounded in the incident, at what the ministry describes as a “vital site”.

However, Iranian state media quotes the military saying there were no offensive or military operations in the region.

“Given the history of hostile actions and the role of the Zionist regime and American forces in using false flags and regional adventures, these accusations are considered a cover for continuing evil and an attempt to increase insecurity in the region,” said Iranian military spokesperson Sardar Shekarchi.

Italy’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation confirmed its citizens’ deaths, saying, “an explosion caused by a drone attack … occurred at a site where two Italian technicians from the company Rheinmetall Italia were working,” with Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani confirming the victims were technicians working at an air-defence surveillance station.

“Regarding the targeting of a vital site in the country as a result of the heinous Iranian aggression, the two injured Italian nationals have died as a result of their injuries,” said Kuwait’s Defence Ministry. It had earlier said the injured were taken to a hospital for treatment while the incident caused unspecified “material damage”.

Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi said the Iranian drone attack happened while the Kuwaiti National Guard and Kuwaiti military were meeting with an Italian delegation that was visiting, including the commander general of the Italian Carabinieri, Lieutenant-General Salvatore Lungo, as well as the Italian ambassador to Kuwait.

Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she was informed of the “tragic deaths”.

“On behalf of myself and the Government, I express my deepest sorrow and extend my heartfelt condolences to the victims’ families,” Meloni wrote on X.

The countries of the Gulf region “have in one voice said an attack against one is an attack against all and have continued to condemn these attacks as a violation of sovereignty”, but we’ve seen an uptick in attacks since September, said Basravi, reporting from Doha.

Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, secretary-general of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), strongly condemned Thursday’s “brutal” attack.

In a statement, Albudaiwi stressed that Iran’s continued attacks on Kuwait, targeting its vital facilities and endangering the lives of civilians, constitute a dangerous escalation and threaten regional security.

There was no immediate comment from Iran regarding the attack.

But it was in line with Tehran’s “policy change”, said Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar, reporting from the Iranian capital.

“Increasingly we have heard from the Iranian officials … saying that this state of no war, no peace cannot remain in place forever, and Iran is working on some military options … to break the status quo,” said Serdar.

The conflict – which began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February – has seen the Gulf states caught in the crossfire, with US military facilities and energy installations on their soil targeted.

The United States and Iran are in a standoff over the vital Strait of Hormuz, with the US military working to escort ships transiting the waterway in defiance of Tehran’s attempts to close the strait.

Thursday’s deadly attack comes days after Kuwait activated its air defences to counter drone strikes launched by Iran – the first since early September.

pending_items.title: Settlers smash foundations of Palestinian family's homes in West Bank
pending_items.content:
JALOUD, West Bank, Nov 26 (Reuters) - Militant Israeli settlers smashed the foundations of two homes belonging to a Palestinian family in the West Bank on Thursday, after settler attacks prevented them from returning to them in defiance of an Israeli court order.

Security cameras showed the settlers brought a bulldozer to the hilltop two-storey houses on either side of a road in the village of Jaloud at around 1 a.m. and spent about an hour damaging the houses. The family said it had been forced out months ago.

In a visit to the area, Reuters reporters saw that the concrete foundations of the homes had been partially broken.

"This latest escalation is a direct consequence of the lack of law enforcement and the sense of impunity enjoyed by the perpetrators," said Ghiath Nasser, a lawyer representing the owners of the houses in court.

The demolition follows a surge of settler violence in which settlers have encroached on Palestinian villages, with an average of 53 settler attacks per week since the start of 2026, according to UN figures.

The Israeli military issued a statement condemning Thursday's attack as “a serious criminal act” and said it was investigating the incident. What appeared to be Israeli security forces were visible visiting the area around the homes.

In most cases, such incidents do not result in prosecution. According to Israeli rights group Yesh Din, 93.6% of investigations into settler violence cases are closed without indictments.

“They want to demolish the houses so that we cannot return to them,” said Wael Tubasi, one of the owners of the homes. He said the deadline for the Israeli military to remove the settlers had passed, but Reuters reporters saw settlers in the area throughout the day.

The Israeli military did not immediately comment on why the settlers had not yet been removed.

Israel occupied the West Bank after a 1967 war, and has built hundreds of settlements there. UN bodies, Palestinians and most countries view the settlements as illegal under international conventions, a stance that is disputed by Israel, and as an obstacle to peace.

The Tubasi family now live in a small house in Jaloud, near the West Bank city of Nablus, with a direct view of the homes they were forced to flee.

For months they have seen settlers move freely through their homes, while living in a small dwelling behind the two houses.

“Even though there is a court order, and the army is required to remove them from the area entirely, not just return us to our homes, it's still not being implemented,” said Tubasi.

In September, after the court order, the Israeli military escorted the family back to their houses. Ten minutes after they arrived, around 200 settlers attacked them, forcing the military and the family to retreat, family members said. The settlers then burned the houses and broke much of the furniture inside, they said, and since then they have been unable to return.

“I'm forbidden from reaching my home, while the settlers have the right to remain inside. What rights are there?” said Aedah Tubasi, Wael’s mother.

In April, settlers built a tent near the Tubasi family's homes. They began attacking the family, set fire to their homes, cut their water and electricity, and blocked roads to the houses, the family said.

After three months, settlers appeared at their door and told them they had an hour to leave or be killed "like the Dawabsheh family," Aedah quoted them as saying.

An 18-month-old child, his mother and father were killed when settlers set fire to the home of the Dawabsheh family in the West Bank village of Duma in 2015.

(Reporting by Pesha Magid, Editing by Timothy Heritage)
